etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Found in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.
Possibly cognate with Old Japanese-derived 幸 (sachi, “a hunting implement”) and Korean 살 (sal, “arrow”).
This reading does not appear to be used in modern Japanese.

etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 綿 /绵 (miɛn, “wool; cotton; soft, downy”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *wata. Cognate with Okinawan 綿 (wata).
Originally referred to any batting or stuffing, which was generally unspun silk. The meaning shifted after the spread of cotton in the Muromachi period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Reduplication of 花(はな) (hana, “flower”) + しい (-shii, adjective-forming suffix).
The hana changes to bana as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 誠實 (MC dzyeng zyit).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Ultimately from Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
This was originally just the intransitive counterpart to transitive verb ayamatsu (spelled either 過つ or 誤つ). Both may derive from classical verb ayamu (spelled either 怪む or 危む), itself derived from stem aya related to ideas of danger, as in terms 危うい (ayaui, “risky, dangerous”), 怪しい (ayashii, “questionable, dubious; clumsy, awkward; foreboding (in a bad way); mysterious, bewitching”).
